bill.title: SAVE Moms and Babies Act of 2025
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
subjects: Drug safety, medical device, and laboratory regulation
bill.officialSummary: Support And Value Expectant Moms and Babies Act of 2025 or the SAVE Moms and Babies Act of 2025 This bill prohibits the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) from approving any new drug (either as a brand-name drug or a generic) intended to terminate a pregnancy and imposes additional restrictions on such drugs that are already approved. Under the bill, an already-approved drug intended to terminate a pregnancy may be dispensed to a patient only with a prescription. Furthermore, the FDA may not approve any labeling change that would authorize (1) using the drug after 70 days of gestation, or (2) dispensing the drug by any means other than in-person administration by the prescribing health care practitioner. The FDA must also impose additional restrictions on such already-approved drugs, including by (1) requiring the prescribing health care practitioner to receive a special certification, (2) prohibiting the practitioner from also acting as the dispensing pharmacist, and (3) requiring the practitioner to have the ability to provide surgical intervention to the patient. The bill also rescinds any investigational use exemption already granted to such a drug if the bill would have prohibited the FDA from granting the exemption. (Currently, the FDA may grant an exemption to certain market approval requirements if a drug is intended solely for use in safety and effectiveness investigations.)

classification.plainSummary: This bill would prohibit the FDA from approving any new drugs intended to terminate pregnancy. For drugs already approved for this purpose, it would impose new restrictions: requiring in-person dispensing by a specially certified practitioner, prohibiting use after 70 days of gestation, and mandating that the practitioner be able to provide surgical intervention. The bill would also prevent practitioners from both prescribing and dispensing these medications.

industries.rationale: The bill directly prohibits approval of new abortion drugs and imposes significant new regulatory restrictions on already-approved drugs in this category.
The bill creates new certification requirements for prescribing practitioners and mandates they have surgical intervention capability, changing practice obligations.

plain.whatItDoes: This bill would ban the FDA from approving any new drug (either as a brand-name drug or a generic) intended to terminate a pregnancy and place additional restrictions on such drugs that are already approved.
plain.whoItTouches: Anyone who fills a prescription. Anyone who takes a medicine.
plain.everydayEffect: If it passed, the change would show up in the price at the pharmacy counter. Nothing has changed yet. Most bills never become law.
plain.source: Reworded from the official summary. Staff at the Congressional Research Service wrote that summary. It is public domain, and the full text of it is further down this page.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
